hero.title: Ocean Data Board
hero.subPre: The third piece of the 'Sky · Earth · Ocean' trilogy—
hero.subPost: to watch the earth, and here we watch the sea: nearshore waves and sea temperature, the observed tide and high/low tide forecast at the San Francisco station, and the El Niño now unfolding.

maxWave.label: Max wave height (5 stations)
maxWave.info: Current max wave height among 5 nearshore points (Qingdao outer sea / Yangtze mouth / Xiamen / Pearl River mouth / Sanya) from Open-Meteo Marine grid forecast

avgSst.label: Avg sea-surface temp
avgSst.info: Arithmetic mean of SST at the 5 nearshore points; SST is a key variable for typhoon genesis and El Niño

tideNow.label: Current tide
tideNow.info: Latest observed water level at the San Francisco station (MLLW datum = Mean Lower Low Water, the common zero for US tide stations)

nextHigh.label: Next high tide
nextHigh.info: NOAA harmonic tide prediction (next 48h); times are in local station time

nextLow.label: Next low tide
nextLow.info: Tidal range = difference between adjacent high and low tides; matters for beachcombing, entering port and avoiding shoals

cyclone.label: Active cyclones
cyclone.info: Number of active cyclones in the NOAA NHC area of responsibility (N Atlantic + NE Pacific); hurricane strength is ≥ 64 kt. NW Pacific typhoons are not in this source

ssta.label: Ocean temp anomaly
ssta.info: Deviation of the global annual mean ocean temperature from the 1901–2000 baseline; over 90% of Earth's trapped heat has gone into the ocean

oni.label: El Niño ONI
oni.info: 3-month running mean of Niño 3.4 SST anomaly; ≥ +0.5 El Niño / ≤ −0.5 La Niña, |ONI|≥2.0 very strong

buoy.label: Max buoy wave (obs)
buoy.info: Largest significant wave height currently observed by the NOAA NDBC global buoy network (distinct from the model-forecast 'max wave height' above)

typhoon.label: W. Pacific Typhoons
typhoon.info: Count of active typhoons located in real time by CMA (China Meteorological Administration); intensity uses a 2-minute average wind, a different basis from NHC hurricanes

footer: All data come from free public APIs (Open-Meteo Marine / NOAA CO-OPS / NOAA CPC / NOAA NHC / NOAA PSL / NOAA NCEI / NOAA NDBC), for science popularization and visualization only. Sea state is a gridded model forecast, not station observations; tide times are local station time; climate oscillation grades follow NOAA official thresholds; active cyclones cover only the NHC area (N Atlantic & NE Pacific); buoys report observed values after each hour, station clocks differ slightly, and missing data are marked MM.

waves.srcNearshore: Open-Meteo Marine (no key), one request for 5 nearshore points, refreshed every 30 min; direction is incoming
waves.panelSwellWind: Swell & Wind Wave: Two Waves in One Sea
waves.tipSwell: Long-period waves from a distant storm; this is why big waves appear even when it is calm locally
waves.tipWindWave: Short-period waves raised by the local wind on the spot; they scatter once the wind dies
waves.prose1: The sea surface is actually the superposition of two wave trains: wind waves are raised by the local wind, chaotic and short-period (3–8 s), and vanish soon after the wind stops; swell is generated by distant storms and travels thousands of kilometres with a regular shape and long period (8–20 s), still lapping the shore on calm, windless days.
waves.prose2: Looking at the two separately explains a common phenomenon: calm and sunny locally, yet big swells rise — that is the precursor swell of an distant ocean storm, arriving days before the storm itself. Surfers wait for it, and it is often the culprit behind broken moorings and violent ship rolling. The 'significant wave height' in the table is the average of the highest 1/3 after the two combine — not the maximum wave height; the actual maximum can reach 1.6–1.9× of it.
waves.srcForecast: Open-Meteo Marine, hourly wave height (gridded reanalysis + forecast model), refreshed every 30 min
waves.srcGlobal: Open-Meteo Marine, one multi-point request for representative global areas, refreshed hourly; times are UTC

tide.srcObs: NOAA CO-OPS tide station 9414290 (San Francisco), 6-min sampling, refreshed every 6 min
tide.srcPred: NOAA CO-OPS harmonic prediction (interval=hilo), refreshed hourly; times are local station time
tide.srcWx: NOAA CO-OPS weather sensor, San Francisco station 9414290, refreshed every 30 min
tide.wxTipTitle: Sea-land temperature difference drives the sea-land breeze: land warms faster by day, wind blows from sea to land; the reverse at night. San Francisco's summer fog comes from this difference
tide.panelDatum: What Does the Tide Datum Mean
tide.prose1a: The zero of a tide table is not sea level but an agreed datum. This station uses
tide.prose1b: — taking the lower of the two daily low waters as the long-term average. US nautical charts and tide tables use it universally, so most observed water levels are positive and there is no confusion from negative tides.
tide.prose2: Note it is not the same as 'Mean Sea Level (MSL)': MSL is the baseline for sea-level-rise research. The MLLW and MSL of the same gauge can differ by over half a metre; crossing datums when quoting tide levels must be converted, or tens of centimetres appear or vanish out of nowhere.

oni.srcOni: NOAA CPC (cpc.ncep.noaa.gov), 3-month running mean of Niño 3.4 SST anomaly, refreshed every 12h
oni.srcSsta: NOAA NCEI Climate at a Glance, global annual mean ocean temp anomaly, baseline 1901–2000
oni.emptySsta: No ocean temp anomaly data yet
oni.sstaTip: 1981–2010 is a common modern climatological reference period; the gap with the last 10 years is the amount of 'acceleration'
oni.captionSsta: Over 90% of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases has gone into the ocean. This curve is the most direct thermometer of 'Earth's energy imbalance' — less disturbed by interannual noise than air-temperature anomaly, and therefore harder to 'whitewash' with short-term fluctuations.
oni.srcOsc: NOAA PSL (psl.noaa.gov) monthly series, missing-value placeholders (PDO −9.90 / AMO −99.99) removed
oni.oscCaption: {name} annual mean (last 60 yr) · latest valid month {ym} ({value}) · only years of same sign imply a phase; a single month's jump needs no interpretation
oni.prose1: A small patch of the equatorial central-eastern Pacific (5°N–5°S, 170°W–120°W), called Niño 3.4. When its SST stays more than 0.5 °C above normal for months, that is El Niño (the Christ child); below normal is La Niña (the girl).
oni.prose2: Though it is only a fraction of a degree of SST difference — the ocean is Earth's largest heat reservoir, and once this patch 'runs a fever', global atmospheric circulation is rewritten: southern China tends to warm winters with floods south and drought north, Australia and Southeast Asia face drought, and Atlantic hurricanes are instead suppressed. The ONI index NOAA updates each quarter is the most important 'thermometer' for global climate prediction.
oni.prose3: PDO and AMO are slower 'background volume knobs': the same-strength El Niño has a stronger impact on North America under the PDO warm phase. So to judge the real impact of an event, view it against the interdecadal background, not just the absolute ONI value.

cyc.srcActive: NOAA NHC (www.nhc.noaa.gov, no key), refreshed every 10 min; N Atlantic & NE Pacific only
cyc.emptyNone: No active tropical cyclones in the N Atlantic & NE Pacific now
cyc.panelTips: Three Things to Know Before Reading This Table
cyc.tip1: ① Limited coverage. This source is the NOAA National Hurricane Center (NHC), responsible only for the N Atlantic and NE Pacific. NW Pacific typhoons are issued by JTWC, the Japan Meteorological Agency and the Central Meteorological Observatory, and are not in this list. 'No active cyclones' does not mean no typhoons globally.
cyc.tip2: ② Different wind units from China. NHC uses knots (kt) and 1-minute sustained wind; China and Japan use m/s and 2-minute sustained wind, while WMO recommends 10-minute. For the same storm, the 1-minute mean is clearly larger than the 10-minute mean — always check the convention before comparing intensity across agencies.
cyc.tip3: ③ Category looks only at wind, not water and rain. The Saffir–Simpson scale is decided solely by wind speed, yet historically the leading cause of tropical-cyclone deaths is storm surge and inland flooding. A slow-moving 'Category 1' storm can cause worse disasters than a fast-passing 'Category 4'.

buoy.srcList: NOAA NDBC latest_obs (latest observation per station, UTC)
buoy.scaleTitle: Where each station's SST sits on the span
buoy.panelWhy: Why This Table Differs from 'Sea State Forecast'
buoy.prose1: Wave heights on the forecast page come from a numerical model (plugging wind field, depth and topography into the wave equation) — smooth and globally covered; this table is what buoys actually measured at sea, reported hourly, with spikes and gaps.
buoy.prose2: Showing missing data as '—' instead of 0 is intentional: NDBC marks missing with MM, and many stations (especially shore stations and foreign meteorological buoys) have no wave sensor at all and would fill the wave column with 0. Treating such 0 as real yields the false impression that 'the world's sea is a mirror'.
buoy.prose3: Of about 870 active stations worldwide, only about a quarter measure waves — ocean observing is far sparser than land weather stations. The S Hemisphere and Indian Ocean are especially thin, which is why forecasts there are less accurate.

ian.title: 2022 · Hurricane Ian
ian.m1Info: Top of the Saffir–Simpson scale; 1-min sustained wind ≥ 70 m/s
ian.m2Info: Made landfall in SW Florida (Cayo Costa) at Category 4
ian.m3Info: Matches the extreme wave band of this board's 'max buoy wave'
ian.desc: Ian rapidly intensified over the warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico, jumping from tropical storm to Category 5 in a single day, and brought devastating storm surge and inland flooding at landfall. It links the NHC live data in the 'Tropical Cyclones' tab with the wave grading of this board's 'max buoy wave': a hurricane is both a wind disaster and a sea-state disaster, and nearshore wave height is often amplified by storm surge.

elnino.title: 2023–2024 · Strong El Niño
elnino.m1Info: Niño 3.4 SST anomaly, reaching the 'strong El Niño' threshold (|ONI|≥2.0)
elnino.m2Info: This board's 'Climate Oscillation' tab flags ONI≥+0.5 in red
elnino.m3Info: Warm winters in East Asia, floods on the Americas' west coast, reduced fisheries in the equatorial Pacific
elnino.desc: Anomalous warming of the equatorial central-eastern Pacific affects global weather through an atmospheric bridge. This board's 'Climate Oscillation' tab plots the ONI curve live, where you can watch this event climb from +0.5 all the way to +2.0 — exactly the evolution from El Niño 'appearing' to a 'strong event'.

indian.title: 2004 · Indian Ocean Earthquake & Tsunami
indian.m1Info: Sumatra subduction megathrust; energy released comparable to tens of thousands of atomic bombs
indian.m2Info: 14 countries around the Indian Ocean; among the deadliest tsunamis in history
indian.m3Info: The tsunami swept the Indian Ocean and even reached Africa's east coast
indian.desc: This disaster directly gave rise to the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System. It shows tsunamis are not only in the Pacific (this board's tsunami sources mainly cover the Pacific centre); any subduction-zone great quake can trigger a transoceanic tsunami. Understanding the causal chain between the 'subduction megathrust quake' in the Earthquake tab and the 'tsunami bulletin' is key to reading this board.

coast.src: Open-Meteo Marine (sorted by current wave height, high to low)
coast.lead: Sorted by current wave height, high to low. At the same height, a shorter period means steeper, choppier waves — so the advice also factors in period, not just the single wave-height number.
coast.tooltip: Swell {swellH} m / {swellP} s, wind wave {windH} m

1.advice: Not advised to put to sea; port work and nearshore activity should be avoided

2.adviceNormal: Small craft cautious, large craft normal
2.adviceSteep: Steep and messy; small craft advised to cancel

3.adviceNormal: Most vessels operate normally; beginners should sail with a crew
3.adviceSteep: Wind-wave dominated, choppy surface; small craft mind the bumps

4.adviceNormal: Good for nearshore activity, diving and small boats
4.adviceSteep: Low waves but short, choppy period; nearshore play fine, small craft slightly bumpy

nodata.advice: No wave height obtained for this area this time

marine.src: Open-Meteo Marine (daily max wave height, local timezone)
marine.lead: The header is the date; the cell is that area's max wave height that day (metres), coloured by sea-state grade. Wave height is the sum of wind waves and swell: wind waves rise and fall with the local wind, while swell is the long wave from a distant storm — which is why it can be swell-heavy at sea even when locally calm and sunny.

seatem.lead1: Sorted by current SST, high to low. {cond}
seatem.lead2: is the empirical threshold for typhoon genesis and maintenance — only waters warmer than it can fuel a typhoon.

chart.waveFcCaption: 24-hour wave-height forecast for each nearshore point (metres) — nearshore waves are mainly shaped by fetch, swell propagation and tide level
chart.tideAria: Observed tide over the past 24 hours
chart.tideCaption: {station} station observed tide over the past 24h (metres, MLLW datum, NOAA CO-OPS 6-min sampling) — semidiurnal tide about 12h25m per cycle, {station} tidal range up to 1.8 m
chart.oniCaption: ONI = 3-month running mean of Niño 3.4 SST anomaly (NOAA CPC). Five consecutive seasons ≥ +0.5 is El Niño, ≤ −0.5 is La Niña; latest now {year} {season}:

seaTempLeadSort: Sorted by current SST, highest first.
seaTempLeadDiff: North–south SST gap is about {diff}°C ({warm} {warmSst}°C vs {cool} {coolSst}°C).
seaTempThresholdNote: 26.5°C is the empirical threshold for typhoon formation and maintenance — only waters warmer than it can supply energy to a typhoon.

typhoon.srcActive: China Meteorological Administration (typhoon.nmc.cn, key-free), refreshed every 15 min; covers the W. Pacific (typhoons affecting China)
typhoon.emptyNone: No active typhoon in the W. Pacific now
typhoon.panelTips: Three things to know before reading this table
typhoon.tip1: ① Different source. This page shows W. Pacific typhoons from the China Meteorological Administration (CMA) — the ones that affect China are all in this basin. The Tropical Cyclones page shows N. Atlantic and E. Pacific hurricanes from NOAA NHC. Together the two pages cover the world’s major tropical cyclones.
typhoon.tip2: ② Different intensity basis. CMA grades a system into six levels by its 2-minute average maximum wind (tropical depression / tropical storm / severe tropical storm / typhoon / severe typhoon / super typhoon), whereas NHC uses a 1-minute average wind and the five-level Saffir–Simpson scale. The same storm can be one category apart between the two agencies — always check the basis before comparing.
typhoon.tip3: ③ Grade looks at wind only. The CMA grade is determined solely by wind speed, yet the real damage usually comes from storm surge and extreme rainfall. A slow-moving “typhoon”-level system can cause worse flooding than a “super typhoon” that passes quickly.
